meta.title: My Autumn Book — Set 3
meta.subject: English Reading
meta.description: Characters, setting, details, and sequencing in 'My Autumn Book'.

questions.question: Who is the main character and narrator in 'My Autumn Book'?
options: A child who explores outside and collects leaves
A green caterpillar looking for a cocoon
questions.explanation: The story is written from the perspective of a child ('I can hardly wait, To go outside and investigate') who collects leaves and makes a scrapbook.

questions.question: Most of the outdoor exploration in the story happens in or around the narrator's garden and nearby trees.
questions.explanation: True. The narrator starts by going to the garden shed and exploring the garden and surrounding trees.

questions.question: Where does the narrator go at the end of the story to make the book?
questions.explanation: The story says: 'I dash up to my room And open the door... I decorate pages, Arrange to make space.'

questions.question: The Blue Jay cries 'Autumn so soon?' because winter is already over.
questions.explanation: False. The Blue Jay is surprised that autumn is arriving so quickly after summer.

questions.question: Which tree wears 'a crown of gold on its head' in the story?
questions.explanation: The poem mentions: 'Aspen, a crown of gold on its head.'

questions.question: The narrator finds a spider spinning a silken thread in a corner of the garden _______.
questions.hint: A small building used for storing tools.
questions.explanation: The poem states: 'In a corner of the garden shed, Spider spins a silken thread.'

questions.question: What is the first thing the narrator does after returning to their bedroom?
options: Empty their pack and spread their collected items on the floor
Draw a picture of a spider
questions.explanation: The poem says: 'I dash up to my room And open the door. Empty my pack, Spread things on the floor.'

questions.question: Sort these trees based on the color their leaves turn in the autumn:
questions.explanation: Ash (yellow) and aspen (gold) turn yellow/gold. Dogwood (crimson/red), maple (red), and oak (rust brown) turn red/brown.

questions.question: The narrator searches high and low and finds leaves from five different trees: ginkgo, willow, elm, birch, and beech.
questions.explanation: True. The poem lists: 'A ginkgo, a willow, An elm, birch, and beech.'

questions.question: Arrange the words to describe the maple tree's autumn color:
questions.explanation: Correct sentence: 'The maple wears red.' This is a detail from the leaf description page.

questions.question: What is the squirrel doing in the yard to prepare for the change in weather?
options: Digging a hole to bury its food treasure
Spinning a silken thread on the fence
Zipping up its warm winter jacket
questions.explanation: The story tells us: 'Squirrel digs a hole to bury its treasure. Squirrel is expecting a change in the weather.'

questions.question: The narrator sees geese honking above as they fly _______ in formation.
questions.explanation: Geese fly south in formation to find warmer weather for winter.

questions.question: Arrange the words to show how the narrator looks for leaves:
questions.explanation: Correct sentence: 'I search high and low.' This means they looked everywhere.

questions.question: When the crickets no longer sing, it means the outside world has turned warm and bright.
questions.explanation: False. When crickets stop singing late at night, the outside world has turned 'cold, black and white' (winter).

questions.question: What is the correct sequence of events when the narrator creates their book?
options: Empty the pack -> Spread things on floor -> Decorate pages -> Arrange in place
Decorate pages -> Empty the pack -> Go outside -> Spread things on floor
Spread things on floor -> Go outside -> Decorate pages -> Zip jacket
Empty the pack -> Go to sleep -> Decorate pages -> Find a ginkgo leaf
questions.explanation: In pages 155 and 157, the narrator first opens the door and empties the pack, spreads things, decorates the pages, and finally arranges everything in place.
